claims.text: The high performance of PGM nanoscale catalysts for ethanol oxidation is governed by adsorbate-induced modulation of active-site electronic structure.
Adsorption of ethanol, acetaldehyde, and acetate induces local electron-density shifts at PGM active sites.
Adsorbate-induced electron-density shifts alter intermediate binding energies and reaction barriers.
This electronic modulation enhances ethanol-oxidation activity, selectivity, and durability.
The baseline catalyst is a nanostructured pure PGM catalyst, such as pure Pt nanoparticles.
Incorporating a small fraction of a less electronegative metal such as Sn or In into the PGM catalyst will perturb its local electronic structure.
The relevant mediator is a change in the local electronic structure of PGM active sites.
The electronic-structure change produces shifts in the binding energies of adsorbed ethanol-derived intermediates.
Adsorption of ethanol and its intermediates dynamically shifts local electron density at active sites.
The adsorbate-induced shift modifies the d-band center.
Modification of the d-band center adjusts the binding energies of reaction intermediates.
Adjusted intermediate binding energies lower barriers for the 12-electron/12-proton ethanol-oxidation process.
Controlled alloying can optimize adsorption-desorption dynamics relevant to catalytic performance.
Relative to pure PGM nanoparticles, the alloyed catalyst should show measurable shifts in the binding energies of adsorbed ethanol-derived intermediates.
Relative to pure PGM nanoparticles, the alloyed catalyst should show higher current density or otherwise improved ethanol-oxidation kinetics.
The alloyed catalyst should exhibit altered product selectivity during ethanol oxidation.
The mechanism should apply under moderate-temperature operando ethanol oxidation in relevant electrolytes.
The mechanism may fail at extreme temperatures, in drastically different solvents, or where ethanol-derived adsorption dynamics differ substantially.
Optimized electronic structure can improve catalyst durability by suppressing metal dissolution or oxidation.
